card: The other water, and the only one of Delhi's two that is still being spent faster than it returns.

answer: Stage of groundwater extraction is how much of the water that refills an aquifer each year is taken back out of it each year, as a percentage. Under 70 per cent an area is classed Safe; above 100 per cent the aquifer is being spent rather than used, because the balance comes out of storage that does not refill. Delhi's figure is 92.1 per cent, against a national average of 60.6.
explainLead: The number is not how much water is down there. It is what share of the annual income is being drawn.
explain: The Central Ground Water Board assesses each block, mandal or taluk separately — 6,762 of them nationally — and for each one estimates two quantities: how much water recharges the aquifer in a year, and how much is extracted from it. The ratio is the stage of extraction, and the category follows from the ratio.

This makes it a flow measurement, not a stock one. An area at 60 per cent is living on its income. An area past 100 per cent is drawing down a balance accumulated over centuries, and the drawdown is invisible until a borewell stops producing and has to be deepened.

Neither figure is metered. CGWB estimates both by a published methodology and calls them assessments, which is the honest description. They are the official numbers and the best that exist; they are not meter readings.

defs.d: A block, mandal or taluk — the geography the category is assigned to. Delhi has 34.
Annual extraction divided by annual extractable resource, as a percentage.
Extraction past 100 per cent of annual recharge. The aquifer is being spent.
Billion cubic metres. The unit the national water budget is written in.

after: Delhi at 92.1 per cent is below the Over-Exploited line as a whole and well above the Safe one, and the aggregate hides the distribution: ten of its thirty-four units are individually Over-Exploited. A city-wide average conceals an emptying aquifer the same way a city-wide air figure conceals a bad monitor.

This is not a legal limit in the sense the air standards are. Nobody is prosecuted at 101 per cent. It is a published categorisation with statutory consequences attached in places — extraction permissions, notified areas — rather than a notified standard.

readHead: How to read it against the river
readLead: Surface water and groundwater are one system, and Delhi's numbers only make sense together.
measure: A city whose river is unusable for most of its length gets its water from somewhere. Part comes from upstream abstraction at Wazirabad — which is why the Delhi stretch has almost no flow left — and part comes from underneath. The two numbers are describing one shortage from two directions.

The assessment is annual and the category is sticky. A unit does not move between Safe and Critical on a wet monsoon; it moves when the multi-year balance moves, which is the right timescale for the thing being measured and a poor one for noticing an emergency.
Recharge is itself affected by what is built on top. Paving a floodplain removes the surface that fed the aquifer beneath it, so extraction and recharge are not independent variables.
cannot: It cannot tell you how much water is left. It is a rate, not a stock, and CGWB does not publish an aquifer volume.
It cannot tell you about quality. Salinity, nitrate, fluoride and arsenic are separate assessments, and a Safe unit can be undrinkable.
It cannot be read at street level. The unit is a block; a single failing borewell is invisible in it and so is a single recovering one.
It is estimated, not metered. Both terms of the ratio are assessments by a published method.
